content: Active tuberculosis (TB) disease is characterized by the presence of clinical signs or symptoms of TB, distinguishing it from latent TB infection (LTBI), which occurs without any symptoms or signs of disease. In this document, the term active TB or TB disease is used to differentiate it from LTBI. In September 2018, countries committed to providing TB preventive treatment (TPT) to at least 30 million individuals by 2022. This included 24 million household contacts of TB patients and 6 million people living with HIV (PLHIV). The World Health Organization (WHO) operational handbook on TB outlines strategies to achieve these goals, emphasizing the importance of fulfilling commitments made at the United Nations High-Level Meeting (UNHLM) on TB. Approximately one-fourth of the global population is estimated to be infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The risk of developing active TB disease after infection depends on several factors, with weakened immune status being the most significant. Most infected individuals remain asymptomatic and non-infectious but carry an increased risk of progressing to active TB disease. On average, 5–10% of infected individuals will develop active TB during their lifetime, with the majority occurring within the first five years after initial infection. Studies indicate that 75% of individuals who develop active TB after exposure to a TB patient do so within one year of the index patient’s diagnosis, and 97% within two years. Molecular studies in low-burden settings have shown that among those who develop TB within 15 years of exposure, the probabilities of disease progression within one, two, and five years are 45%, 62%, and 83%, respectively. High-risk groups for TB include PLHIV, individuals in contact with TB patients, and those with immunodeficiency conditions. These groups are prioritized for TPT. However, current biomarkers and tests for TB infection cannot distinguish between recent and remote infections. Eligibility for TPT relies on ruling out active TB disease through clinical and radiological evaluation, particularly in high-risk populations. The WHO End TB Strategy prioritizes TPT as a key intervention under its first pillar, focusing on high-risk populations. Programmatic management of TPT (PMTPT) is integrated into broader preventive actions, including TB screening, infection control, HIV care, and access to universal health care. The strategy aims for 90% TPT coverage among PLHIV and household contacts of TB patients by 2025. PMTPT is also critical for low TB burden countries pursuing TB elimination. Despite gradual global expansion of TPT services, access remains limited. By 2022, only 8 million PLHIV, 350,000 children under five, and nearly 80,000 individuals aged five and above were reported to have received TPT. Coverage among household contacts remains particularly low, necessitating urgent action to meet UNHLM targets. Achieving these targets requires significant expansion of TPT services, health system strengthening, and mobilization of human and financial resources. Ministries of health must urgently redesign PMTPT programs and align them with the latest WHO guidelines. This includes adopting a cascade of care approach to systematically identify at-risk individuals, ensure access to TPT, and reduce TB transmission. Key steps in the cascade of care include initial testing, medical evaluation, treatment recommendation, and therapy completion. However, significant losses occur at each step, with less than 20% of eligible individuals completing the entire cascade. These losses are even higher in resource-constrained settings. To address these challenges, national programs and stakeholders must enhance service delivery for target populations. This involves strengthening each element of the cascade of care, from identifying target populations to providing preventive treatment. TPT services should be integrated with TB case-finding efforts, ensuring that presumptive TB patients receive diagnostic testing and treatment if necessary. Individuals without active TB should be evaluated for TB infection and offered TPT. Retention and referral systems must be improved to ensure that individuals evaluated for TB are initiated on TPT and complete treatment. This will reduce the reservoir of TB infection and prevent progression to active disease. The WHO operational handbook provides guidance on policy considerations, health system requirements, and investment areas for scaling up TPT services. It also includes monitoring and evaluation indicators to track progress and support country efforts to achieve global TPT targets. Key recommendations for TPT include offering treatment to PLHIV, household contacts of TB patients, and other high-risk groups. For PLHIV, TPT should be provided as part of comprehensive HIV care, including for those on antiretroviral therapy (ART), pregnant women, and individuals previously treated for TB. Household contacts of bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB patients, particularly children under five, should also receive TPT. In high-risk settings, preventive treatment may be considered for contacts of multidrug-resistant TB patients based on individualized risk assessment. Systematic LTBI testing and treatment are recommended for individuals initiating anti-TNF treatment, those undergoing dialysis, organ or hematological transplant candidates, and individuals with silicosis. It may also be considered for prisoners, health workers, immigrants from high TB burden countries, homeless individuals, and people who use drugs. However, systematic testing is not recommended for individuals with diabetes, harmful alcohol use, tobacco smokers, or underweight individuals unless they belong to other high-risk groups. Screening algorithms should be used to rule out active TB disease before initiating TPT. For PLHIV, those without symptoms such as cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats are unlikely to have active TB and should be offered TPT. Chest radiography may be used to exclude active TB in PLHIV on ART, with TPT provided to those with no abnormal findings. Infants and children living with HIV who exhibit poor weight gain, fever, or cough should also be evaluated for TB and offered TPT if active disease is excluded.
